column3: Here are 15 cold email frameworks mapped directly to 3 awareness levels to use in Claude Code:
column11:
Here are 15 cold email frameworks mapped directly to 3 awareness levels to use in Claude Code:

The biggest cold email mistake isn't a bad framework.

It's using it on the wrong buyer.

Eugene Schwartz figured this out in 1966.
15 cold email frameworks map directly to 3 awareness levels.
Most people pick one they like and run it on everyone.

Here is which one to use and when:

Problem Aware → they know something's wrong, don't know solutions exist

↳ Josh Braun "Write a Good Cold Email" → name the exact problem, don't pitch, don't explain
↳  Vin Matano 🐝 "Leader Responsibilities" → make them curious about their own role, no solution mentioned
↳ Patrick Trümpi "Challenge of Similar Companies" → show them they're not alone with this problem
↳ Keenan (Gap Selling) → show the gap between where they are and where they need to be
↳ ☠️ Belal Batrawy "Mic Drop Method" → permission, problem, provoke, promise

Solution Aware → they're comparing options, probably talking to 3 other people right now

↳ Thibaut Souyris "Do the Math" → put numbers to it, let them run the calculation
↳ Chelsea Castle "Neutral Insight" → hand them a 3rd party stat that reframes the conversation
↳ Jordan Crawford "Upfront Value" → give something useful before you ask for anything
↳ Matt Dixon (Challenger Sale) → teach them something they didn't know, then connect it to you
↳ Todd Caponi "The Transparency Sale" → open with your biggest weakness, trust builds faster than you think

Most Aware → they've seen you, they know you, just haven’t made the next step

↳ Guillermo Blanco "Short Trigger" → 30 words max, name the exact signal, nothing else
↳ 💜 🔮 Will Allred "Ask Before Pitch" → one direct question
↳ Bow Tied Sales Guy "Not Too Different Persona" → you're just like them, peer framing
↳ Chris Voss (Never Split the Difference) → one open question, empathy, and stop there
↳ Becc Holland "Flip the Script" → say out loud what they're already thinking about you

My tip for you:

Don't pick your favourite framework.
Pick the framework that matches where the buyer is.

column3: B2B GTM in 2026 looks nothing like 2021.
column11:
B2B GTM in 2026 looks nothing like 2021.

In 2021: SDRs first, data later. In 2026: signals first, SDRs last (most of them are enabled with AI).

Here is the new 5-layer order:

1. Build out the foundation
↳ Say your ICP pain out loud: repeat their pain in their own words
↳ Clarify your offer: Scaling a weak offer produces a lot of noise and no recurring revenue
↳ Name your enemy: give buyers something to remember you against
↳ Stack signals: funding round + GTM hire + engaged your content = one outreach trigger
↳ Protect the inbox: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain warm-up, copy never gets read from spam

Tools we usually connect here:
Clay, Apify, Trigify, Common Room, Cognism , Demandbase , Warmly, 

2. Strategize
↳ Let triggers write the copy: company hires a GTM engineer? That IS the email
↳ Run multiple channels: Content builds awareness. Outbound activates intent. Ads reinforce both.
↳ Narrow down your ICP: “B2B SaaS ” is a category vs. ”Series A SaaS with an existing inbound team” is a real target.
3. Execute

↳ Content: Builds the audience before outreach ever starts.
↳ Signal‑based outbound: Reach out when something actually happened.
↳ Retargeting Ads should follow engagement, not random targeting.

Tools here usually look like:
lemlist, EmailBison, Expandi, LinkedIn Ads, ZenABM , Unify, Cargo, Default

We systemize these to make sure they compound.

4. Amplify
↳ Boost posts that already booked meetings, don't guess what to pay to promote
↳ Repurpose your best-performing content into content-led outbound sequences
↳ Run lookalike campaigns against your closed-won accounts

Stack we use:
Dock, HubSpot , Fellow AI

5. Scale
↳ Systematize what worked: document the triggers, the copy, the list criteria
↳ Add channels only after layers 1 and 2 are solid
↳ Replace manual steps with agents once the process proves out

Pipeline compounds when the foundation is right.
Most teams are building from layer 3 up (activation). That’s why it doesn’t work:

You can’t build the roof on the house if the floors are missing:

Foundation = data.
Architecture = signals + enrichment.
Activation = manual (SDRs, AEs) + AI SDRs.
GTM Copilot = the final layer, once the system runs itself

column3: "What's the best GTM channel?" Wrong question.
column11:
"What's the best GTM channel?" Wrong question.

The real question is: How do you build a system where every motion makes the next one cheaper and better, so your GTM can compound over time?

Here's how we think about the 2026 Growth Loop:

1. Generate demand
content, paid, outbound, and partnerships. Where does your buyer actually spend time? start there, not everywhere.

2. Identify who's paying attention 
to lead magnets, forms, social engagement, and organic followers. If traffic doesn't turn into something you own, it disappears.

3. Stay in the room SDR
sequences, newsletter, community, events, retargeting. Most of the pipeline you need this quarter is already in your database. 
They're just not ready yet.

4. Earn the trust, 
sales-led: get the call booked. product-led: get them to first value. Before either happens, they've already read your case studies, watched your demo, and used your free tool.

5. Score and route automatically 
Clay and HubSpot score every inbound signal against your ICP. High fit goes to sales immediately. Low fit goes back into nurture. 90% of this doesn't need a human in the loop anymore.

6. Land & Expand Retention 
is underrated as a growth channel. Clients who stay become your case studies. Case studies become your best top-of-funnel.

Why the whole thing compounds over time:

Cold outreach converts better when prospects already recognise the brand.

The content that performs organically tells you what to put a budget behind.

Your paid audiences and your outbound lists overlap more than most people realise & every engagement signal from every stage sharpens the next campaign.

We use HubSpot and Clay to handle scoring and routing in stage 5, CommonRoom, Trigify.io, and Factors.ai AI to pick up 1st-party engagement signals in stage 2, and Kit to keep the nurture motion running in stage 3, so each one is making the next stage more efficient.

not every path needs to be running. 
but every stage should have at least one.

but you need to orchestrate and connect the dots between sales and marketing to make customer acquisition effective.

which one is the gap in yours right now?

7 questions. Every discovery call. Real-time AI scoring after every one. Here’s the exact framework:

The 7 questions we ask every prospect:

Question 1: "What made you reach out right now?"
↳ By the time they call, they've already done 70% of the research. If they can not answer this in one sentence, they are not ready.

Question 2: "What does your current go-to-market motion look like?"
↳ You need to know what is running and how it is working and set up before you propose anything.

Question 3: "What has not worked?"
↳ They will tell you exactly what not to sell them.

Question 4: "Who else is involved in this decision?"
↳ A deal that stalls always stalls because of someone you never met.

Question 5: "What does success look like in 90 days?"
↳ Specific. A number if possible. This becomes your proposal framing.

Question 6: "What happens if this does not get solved this quarter?"
↳ Tells you how much urgency they actually feel, not how much they say they feel.

Question 7: "Is there anything that would stop this from moving forward?"
↳ Every unspoken objection lives in the answer to this question.

What happens when the call ends:

Fellow - AI Meeting Assistant transcribes the full call automatically. (this can be Gong , Otter)
Claude and Clay read the transcript and scored it across four dimensions:

↳ ICP fit: firmographic + pain match

↳ Stakeholder map: who is in the room and who is missing?
↳ Package fit: Which GT service matches what they described

The output: a one-page brief. Package recommendation. Next step. Handed to sales as a review before the follow-up goes out, and for sales coaching purposes.

We get 50% of our clients through LinkedIn.
Here’s how to capture them and start a conversation with them:

Most prospects don’t book immediately.
They read, listen, and engage first.

At Growth Today, we see it every week with new clients: the warm signals are there.

The way to achieve the same is simple.
Here's the 5-step framework:

1. Capture across channels (not just LinkedIn)
↳ LinkedIn: profile views, comments, likes, connection requests
↳ Website: anonymous visitors ( Snitcher  ), pricing page hits, competitor comparison visits
↳ Content: who's reading your stuff (Trigify / Expandi / Vector 👻  / CommonRoom)
↳ Account-level: job changes in the buying committee (Clay / Champify )
↳ Email: opens, clicks, repeat reads in your sequencer

2. Stack the signals (if you have a very strong inbound motion, otherwise skip)
↳ 1 signal = reason to reach out
↳ 3+ signals from the same account = prioritize
↳ Multiple people from the same company = absolutely prioritize
↳ Track signal velocity (how fast multiple signals appear on one account)

3. Qualify against ICP
↳ Role + seniority match
↳ Company fit (size, industry, stage)
↳ Buying authority + buying committee structure

4. Reference the insight (not the signal)
↳ Reference the specific insight (if make sense)
↳ Don't pretend you don't know they engaged
↳ Keep it short, contextual, and low-pressure
↳ Multi-thread the account (if the top account + multiple engagements have happened)

5. Track the right metrics
↳ Chat-to-response and response to meeting conversion rate
↳ Signal velocity (signal → meeting time)
↳ Signal source mix (LinkedIn vs website vs content vs email)
↳ Account-level pipeline coverage from signals

Familiarity drives the B2B pipeline.
Cold lists alone don't.

1. One idea. Full stop.

↳ Not five insights crammed into one frame
↳ Not a paragraph disguised as a bullet
↳ One claim, one proof, one visual

If a reader can’t understand it in 3 seconds, they scroll.

2. Structure before design

↳ The headline carries the post, not the typography
↳ Every line on the graphic supports the headline
↳ The takeaway is visible instantly

Design should amplify the idea.

Do not replace it.

3. Scannable at a glance

↳ Headline sits in the top third of the visual
↳ Max ~30 words on the graphic
↳ Eye flows vertically, not across
↳ White space is structure, not decoration

Most posts fail here.

4. A reason to save

↳ A checklist
↳ A framework
↳ A repeatable process
↳ Something useful in 3 weeks

If someone can’t explain why they saved it, they won’t save it.

Good design gets attention.
Good structure gets results.

Most GTM graphics have the first.
Almost none have both.

column3: COLD EMAIL FUNDAMENTALS. 6 patterns that separate the top 1% from everyone else:
column11:
COLD EMAIL FUNDAMENTALS. 6 patterns that separate the top 1% from everyone else:

A few of our customers send 750,000 emails/mo. Others targeting the enterprise send between 27,000 and 50,000 emails/month.

Here are the 6 things that the top-performing teams we work with do differently:

1. Strong offer + clear ICP

↳ Specific pain + clear ROI + proof + risk reversal.
↳ Clearly defined ICP related to industry, role, trigger, and pain.
↳ Pain is also clearly written out and translated into triggers (e.g., funding, 10K), and behavioral signals (e.g., ad engagements, social)

2. Strong data foundation

↳ Beyond name + email: LinkedIn profile, department, headcount, tech stack overlap, job postings, funding signals.

If you want to personalize your emails at scale, you need proper data at scale first.

3. AI-personalized openers

↳ Reference one specific thing, such as a job posting, funding round, case study, tech stack item, or recent product launch.

Every email should feel 1:1, not 1:1000.

4. Fundamentals before fancy tactics

↳ Three pillars drive 80% of performance: ICP, Offer, Copy.
↳ Nail these before any fancy tactics or tooling.

5. Smaller, tiered lists > 100k

↳ Tier 1: 30-50 dream accounts. Tier 2: 200 ICP-fit accounts.
↳ Smaller lists = deeper research per lead + better deliverability + higher reply rates.

6. Give value in emails [HIGH IMPACT]

→ Lead with insight, a teardown, or a Loom. The ask comes later.

❌ "Got 15 min for a demo?"
❌ Feature dump + calendar link in email 1
✅ "Can I send over a mockup of our funnels so you can take a look and decide?
✅ "Recorded a 4-min Loom of how to monetize your social followers. Can I send it over?"

7. Follow up fast + contextually

→ Day 0 (Email 1): personalized opener + value offer
→ Day 3 (Email 2): short follow-up, single new insight
→ Day 6 (Email 3): new angle or extra value
→ Day 10 (Email 4): break-up, low pressure (e.g reference their colleague, ask for a better person to contact, etc.)

Most replies come from follow-ups.

8. Long-term play, not one-shot

↳ Compound growth engine = strong data foundation + clear ICP + crisp messaging matrix.

If any GTM channel worked with quick wins, everybody would have an IPO.
Play the long-term game. No shortcuts.

9. Manage deliverability [CRITICAL]

↳ Clean validated list.
↳ SPF, DKIM, DMARC.
↳ Multiple domains for backup.
↳3 inboxes per domain.
↳ <3% bounce rate.
↳ 5-20 emails per inbox per day.
↳Automated inbox placement tests.

Where conversations stalled

Make Learning as the #1 KPI if you are building your outbound motion scratch.

When something started performing, we documented it.
Targeting logic. Deliverability standards. Messaging patterns based on real conversations.

↳ claude.ai/install or `brew install --cask claude-code`

2️⃣ CLAUDE.md → your operating system
Without it: generic AI.
With it: expert in your stack, your rules, your workflows, and what’s your role in the organization (saved in the memory)

↳ `./CLAUDE.md` → each repo
↳ `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` → global rules
↳ `.claude/rules/` → path-specific rules

Keep it under 200 lines. Clear. Direct. Specific.

Claude reads the description and decides which skill to use. You don't call them manually or using the / unless you want to enforce it.

We have 50+ skills at Growth Today:
↳ GTM playbook generation
↳ Signal-based outbound frameworks
↳ Data enrichment workflows with Clay
↳ Campaign copy and design briefs
↳ Client onboarding

Skills handle knowledge. MCP handles actions.

↳ Claude mcp add --transport http [name] [url]`
↳ HubSpot , Gmail, Slack, Sheets, databases (will cover 80% of your GTM use cases)
↳ Scope by: local, project, or user

5️⃣ Hooks → fires on events

↳ PreToolUse → block risky commands
↳ PostToolUse → auto-format code
↳ SessionStart → reload your context
↳ Notification → desktop alerts

We use N8N for automated inbox placement test and adjust the daily cold + warmup settings based on the recent email health results.

8️⃣ Useful Slash commands
↳ `/init` → build CLAUDE.md from your existing code
↳ `/compact` → clear bloated context
↳ `/memory` → check what Claude remembers
↳ `/cost` → track token spend live
↳ `/review` → pull request review

↳ `claude -n "feature-name"` → start fresh
↳ `claude -c` → continue last session
↳ `claude -r "project-name"` → jump back in
↳ `claude --fork-session` → branch your work

Tip: One session per feature. Commit to Git before you switch.

9️⃣ CLI flags for headless and automation mode
↳ `claude -p "query"` → one-shot runs, plug into scripts and CI
↳ `claude --add-dir ../other-repo` → merge context from another repo
↳ `claude --effort high` → deep thinking mode
↳ `claude --max-budget-usd 5` → hard spend cap
↳ `claude --permission-mode plan` → read-only, no edits

We use headless mode to run our prospecting engine and ship mini-tools that capture leads. 50+ skills handle everything from GTM playbook generation to client onboarding.

column3: Stop editing cold email copy to fix reply rates. 16% of legitimate B2B emails never reach the inbox in 2026 (Validity). Here’s what to do instead:
column11:
Stop editing cold email copy to fix reply rates. 16% of legitimate B2B emails never reach the inbox in 2026 (Validity). Here’s what to do instead:

1. Monitor Inbox placements weekly
Validity tracked 16.5% of legit B2B emails going to spam in 2026.
Test with GlockApps, MailReach , or Instantly, Smartlead's built-in tool weekly

↳ Stop guessing. Test the actual placement.

2. SPF, DKIM, DMARC
If you don't set this up, your inbox will get a HUGE spam rate within 2-3 weeks of sending.

↳ Run a check with MX Toolbox, GSuite, Instantly, Smartlead's checker before the next campaign.

4. Move DMARC from p=none to p=reject within 90 days
Most teams set DMARC to p=none (monitoring only) and never enforce.
Inbox providers flag domains stuck on none because spoofers love them.

↳ Move to p=quarantine after 30 days, p=reject after 90

5. Use the secondary domain, never the primary.
Sending cold from your primary domain is how you can get your domain burnt, negatively impacting your day-to-day business.

↳ Buy secondary domains, never use your primary domain for cold emails

6. 2 inboxes per secondary domain
Gmail and Outlook flag domains with too many senders. Cap at 2 per domain. So if you want 12 active inboxes, you need 6 secondary domains. Not 1 domain with 12 mailboxes.

↳ 2 inboxes at domains gets you 10 inboxes to start.

7. Warmup 2-4 weeks before the first cold send
Brand new domain sending 50 cold emails on day one is a death sentence. Warm up 4-8 weeks before launch using Instantly, Smartlead. Yes, this means waiting; there's no shortcut.

↳ 2 - 4 weeks of warmup w/o cold emailing.

8. 5-20 cold emails per inbox per day. No spikes.
Spikes look like spam. 200 emails Monday and 20 Tuesday flags you faster than a steady 20 a day. Both Instantly and Smartlead auto-throttle for a reason. Use it.

↳ Consistent low sending > spikes burning your inboxes

9. Bounce rate under 2%
Verify 100% of your list with MillionVerifier , MailNinja, lemlist  and ZeroBounce before any send. If the list is older than 30 days, re-verify it.

↳ Re-validate any lists older than 30 days. Always.

10. Plain text only. No HTML, no images, no tracking pixels.
HTML emails read as marketing emails to Gmail's filters.

↳ If you wouldn't type it as a Slack DM to a coworker, don't send it cold.

Infrastructure is responsible 99% of your results. If your email is in spam, the copy, your offer, simply doesn't matter.

column3: A no from last quarter is not a no today.

A no from last quarter is not a no today.
Budget freed up, the champion got promoted, the blocker left. 
Here is how we catch that and reopen the deal:

It is not that teams do not know the deals are worth reopening.

It is just often a random activity when 1) pipeline is dry 2) team not hitting the quarterly plan 3) being asked to do so

instead of having a clear structure system + cadence to make sure this isn’t forgotten 👀

So we stopped treating it as someone's job to remember and built it into the system.

Here is the system we run:

1. Pull your closed-lost from the last 6 to 12 months

↳ They had a budget and a need once, which does not disappear
↳ This list is already in your CRM, free, and sitting there

2. Pull the reason each one stalled

↳ the call notes and the transcript, the exact objection in their words
↳ no budget, no champion, wrong time, lost to a competitor

3. Watch for the reason to expire

↳ new funding, a new leader in the buyer seat, a hiring spike, and a competitor they left
↳ The blocker that killed the deal is often gone now

4. Score and tier by what changed

↳ Tier 1 is the deals where the reason for no is gone
↳ Tier 2 is something moved but not the blocker
↳ Tier 3 is still cold. Leave it
↳ hours of digging turn into minutes

5. Reopen with the real reason, not a check-in

↳ "Last year, the timing was off because of the reorg. That settled, so worth another look?"
↳ Name the old objection and what changed, never "just circling back"

The fix is not a better reminder. It is taking the maybe out of someone's head and putting it in a system that watches for you. Owners change. The system does not.

LinkedIn outbound is not email outbound. The inbox is shorter. The preview is meaner. The "Hi {firstname}, I saw your profile and thought we could chat" template that worked for cold email gets you ignored on LinkedIn .

Here is the 6-line LinkedIn DM structure that books meetings:

Line 1: The signal opener
↳ Reference something they did in the last 30 days
↳ Hiring posts, podcast appearances, funding rounds, and new role announcements
↳ Bad: "I saw your profile and thought..."
↳ Good: "Saw you just hired your first GTM engineer."

Line 2: The relevance bridge
↳ Connect the signal to a pain they actually feel
↳ One sentence. No second clauses.
↳ Bad: "I wanted to reach out because we work with companies like yours."
↳ Good: "Most new GTM engineers spend month 1 untangling the existing stack."

Line 3: The credibility line
↳ One concrete data point. No hype words.
↳ Bad: "We are the leader in GTM solutions."
↳ Good: "We have worked with similar companies like {Similar Brand}"

Line 4: The micro-ask
↳ Lowest friction next step. Not a calendar link.
↳ Bad: "Got 15 minutes for a call this week?"
↳ Good: "Could I send you the 4-page audit template we use?"

Line 5: The optional out
↳ Give them permission to say no
↳ Good: "If not the right time, no worries."

Line 6: The sign-off
↳ One word. Your first name.
↳ No "kind regards, looking forward to hearing from you"

3 LinkedIn-specific mistakes that kill reply rates:

1. The wall of text
↳ LinkedIn DMs preview the first 60 characters in the inbox
↳ If line 1 does not earn the open, line 6 does not matter
↳ Keep total LinkedIn DM length under 600 characters

2. The calendar link in message 1
↳ LinkedIn flags Calendly URLs in cold DMs as a spam signal
↳ Reply rates drop 60% when a calendar link is in the first DM
↳ Lead with a resource, not a meeting

3. The connection note plus DM stack
↳ Sending a connection note AND a follow-up DM in the same hour reads as automated
↳ Wait 2 to 3 days between the connection note and the first LinkedIn DM
↳ Treat them as two separate touches, not one sequence

If you know your ICP and run this 6-line structure across 200 LinkedIn DMs a week, you could really get a 12% reply rate and get more meetings. Same ICP. More relevant messaging structure.

53 campaigns. 37 with issues. 3 were copy problems. Here’s what the other 34 had in common and how to fix these in 7 days:

Day 1: Fix the list
↳ Stop filtering just by job title and company size
↳ Go back to your last 10 closed deals and find what they actually had in common (HubSpot, Salesforce)

What we actually look at:
↳ Which personas are associated with the deals vs. booked a call
↳ Whether the contact is an influencer, a champion, or an end user (each needs a completely different message)
↳ Whether this is a Tier 1 account (strong signal, high ICP fit) or Tier 2 (weaker signal, worth warming up first)
↳ What their buying journey looks like before they come to you: Do they run a trial, or download content first?

Day 2: Fix deliverability
↳ Check whether your emails are landing in the inbox at all
↳ Adjust the cold + warm-up daily volume based on this.

Day 3: Fix the offer
↳ Ask yourself: how useful am I actually being to this person?
↳ An audit, a checklist, a resource, a teardown. Something real. Something useful.

Day 4: Fix the CTA
↳ One ask per email. Make it easy to say yes.

But the ask has to match the account:
↳ High engagement + Tier 1 → reach out directly. These are your highest-value shots.
↳ Re-engaged + Tier 2 → still worth a direct touch, but with a softer ask.
↳ Low engagement, any tier → push them into nurture or LinkedIn audience first. Do not waste a direct ask on a cold account and on a cold signal.

We use Clay to push them directly to the ad audience, so you can get 80% better match rate.
The less engaged the contact, the more you need to warm them before you ask.

Day 5: Fix personalization
↳ Stop personalizing based on company description
↳ Personalize based on the signal that triggered the outreach and job title/bio

Day 6: Fix the sequence
↳ Adjust the sequence structure: SMB vs. Mid-market.
↳ Differentiate: Omnichannel (High engagement +high tier) vs. Multichannel vs. email-only (lemlist, EmailBison, Instantly.ai, or Smartlead)

Day 7: Fix what you measure
↳ Inbox placement rate, positive reply rate, meetings per 1,000 sends
↳ Open rate tells you almost nothing

If I had to pick one to fix first: the offer.

The question is not "how do I write a better email"
The question is "how do I become genuinely useful to this person."
Answer that. Then write the email.

column3: What are the metrics I should actually care about when launching vs scaling your outbound program?
column11:
What are the metrics I should actually care about when launching vs scaling your outbound program?

I see a lot of “we booked 100 meetings in 7 days” screenshots with no context. Over-inflated promises. It sets founders and reps up for disappointment.

So let me give you the real benchmarks 👀

———

🖊️ REPLY RATE

What good looks like: 1–5%
What I see people claim: 15–20%

Is that doable? Yes. When you hyper-focus on a tiny segment.

Example: I worked with a client where we hit 8–9% response rate with 30% positive response rate. But we were targeting 2000 people out of a million in their TAM.

Super segmented. Super unique copy.
You cannot scale that. You cannot send that super-targeted message to a million people because 80% of your prospects don’t have those “intels” that 
you used to send that super-targeted messaging.

So in the grand scheme of things?
Expect 1–5%.


———

💜 POSITIVE RESPONSE RATE
This is the percentage of responses that are actually useful.

Most replies are “remove me”, “not the right person”, OOO, or pure noise.
Those don't count.

Positive replies are:

“Tell me more” “How is this different from X?” “Can you send the audit?” 

“Here’s my Calendly”

What good looks like: 10–30% positive out of all real replies
Best case (hyper-segmented): up to 50%

If you only track two metrics, make it these two.

They tell you if:
list is right offer is relevant timing makes sense

———

🔨 BOUNCE RATE (health metric)
This is not a “copy” problem. It is a data + email infrastructure problem.

High bounces mean:

bad or inaccurate enrichment people left the orgs you’re trying to reach weak data vendors risky domains

What good looks like: below 1%
Tolerable: 3% (max 5%)

More than that and you burn your domains, hurt deliverability so none of your emails will reach your prospects.

———

And open rates?
Nice to look at, but not where I start. Vanity metrics. Doesn’t tell you ANYTHING.

For every outbound system we build at Growth Today, we first make sure:

clean + accurate data (= data foundation) stable infra (= scalable email infrastructure) clear offer (= value you can give to your prospects in exchange of their time speaking to you)

Then we watch these 3:

reply rate positive reply rate bounce rate

column3: One of your lowest-hanging fruit in outbound?
column11:
One of your lowest-hanging fruit in outbound?

Knowing timing with relevancy beats everything.

Which is exactly why signal-based, always-on outbound is such an easy win. 🏆

Most teams still run prospecting like this:
Build → send → finish → rebuild → repeat.

We’ve all done it.

But that approach makes it almost guaranteed you’ll miss people at the right time.

Because readiness rarely lines up with when you decide to run a campaign.

It usually shows up when something shifts on their side:

• budget changes 
• new leadership 
• pressure to hit numbers 
• new goals 
• new problems

Here’s what that means in practice 👇

1️⃣ Signals can tell you WHO is ready, not just who “fits the ICP.”

Two companies can look identical on paper.

But only one is:

- hiring for Demand Gen
- posting thought leadership
- running new ads
- adding new leaders
- changing their GTM team
- promoting new initiatives

One is active.
The other is static.

Usual prospecting motion treats everyone the same.
Signal-based outbound differentiates who’s ready and who’s not.

2️⃣ You stop “guessing” and start “reacting.”

When a new VP joins…
When a Head of Events gets hired…
When a team scales ad spend…
When leadership suddenly becomes very active online…

That’s your window.
Not next quarter.
Not “when we build the next list.”
Right. Then.

Outbound that responds to real changes simply feels more relevant, because it is.

3️⃣ Your messaging becomes naturally relevant

You don’t need hyper-personalization.
You just need context.

Examples we used:

“Saw you’re hiring for Event Marketing — usually means the team is thinking a lot about pipeline. Could I share a few ideas?”

“Congrats on the new senior hire — would a few simple recommendations around X be helpful?”

“Noticed your ad spend is climbing — if mainstream channels aren’t giving you what you need, I can send a quick idea that’s been working well for 
similar teams.”

When you know who you’re talking to and what they’re dealing with, the message almost writes itself, especially when you offer something tangible.

4️⃣ You stop exhausting the TAM

Usual prospecting motion = you work the static list you already have.
Signal-based outbound = you run always-on campaigns and surface new leaders, new accounts, and new activity as it happens.

It’s easier on the TAM and better for long-term performance.

5️⃣ Conversion rates lift without changing the copy

This is the part people underestimate.
Same message. Same CTA. Same structure.

But when it hits at the right time, the response rate looks completely different.

TAKEAWAY 🤩

Outbound is hard, and not getting easier
…and there are SO many gimmicks and so many tactics

but you cannot disagree that it’s a good idea to reach out to a prospect when there’s a real moment to do so ✌️

column3: Hot take, but CTAs are one of the biggest reasons outbound underperforms 👀
column11:
Hot take, but CTAs are one of the biggest reasons outbound underperforms 👀

Not because the prospect hates meetings.
But because the CTA gives them zero reason to say yes. 🙅‍♀️

Welcome to commoditization.

It’s what happens when 100s of agencies and SaaS tools all promise the same thing, in the same way, at roughly the same price.

Last week, while rebuilding a services company’s outbound motion, this became painfully obvious.

Their CTA was: “Open to a quick chat?” “Would you be open to exploring how {outcome}?

Everyone uses that line.

In commoditized markets, a meeting is work for the buyer.
Your CTA gives them no reason to say yes.

Here’s how to change that👇

1️⃣ In a commoditized market, your CTA is your differentiation

If your offer sounds like:

“We lower your CAC.”
“We scale your Meta ads.”
“We run data-backed performance campaigns.”
…congrats, you’re in one of the most commoditized categories on earth. 😅

2️⃣ Value-first CTAs instantly reposition you

Instead of:
“Let me pitch you,”

It becomes: “Here’s something useful I put together for you.” which read in the prospect's mind like this: “Even if we don’t end up working together, I’ve got something useful

If I were running an ad agency, these would be one of the 20 CTAs I’d test to start conversations with my prospects:

Performance / Paid Media CTAs
“I reviewed your last 90 days of ad performance. Can I send a quick summary over?”
“I spotted a few creative angles that could bring costs down. Could I share those ideas?”
“I noticed opportunities to simplify your structure. Would a short outline be helpful?”

Creative Strategy CTAs
“I pulled the hooks performing best in your niche. Could I send your custom list?”
“I mocked up three new creative variations based on your current ads. Can I share them?”
“I found a few reasons why your creatives may be fatiguing early. Would insights help?”

Landing Page / CRO CTAs
“I ran a quick heatmap pass on your hero section. Can I send the notes?”
“I drafted a few landing page revisions that may lift conversions. Should I send a preview?”
“I did a scroll-depth check on your offer page. Could I share what stood out?”

Full-Funnel / Growth CTAs
“I mapped a few friction points across your funnel. Can I send the snapshot?”
“I created a simple revenue path model for brands at your scale. Should I send it over?”
“I drafted a new offer angle based on recent trends. Would it be helpful if I shared it?”

5️⃣ Why this matters more in the (ad) agency world

In performance marketing, EVERYONE claims they do:
creative strategy
media buying
funnel optimization
offer testing
attribution
scaling frameworks

When done right, your CTA becomes the most differentiated part of your entire outbound motion.

TAKEAWAY:

Your CTA is the first place your differentiation shows up, or doesn’t.
….& this is SO EASY to implement and TEST what works! ✌️

More human and more useful from the very first touchpoint.

One thing I love about outbound is how quickly the truth shows itself.
If the system is off, the results will slow down.

If the system is right, everything works

Last week we worked with a services company whose outbound didn’t have too many results But once we dug in, the problem wasn’t just the list or the copy …it was that their system was fighting against them.

Here’s exactly what we changed:

1️⃣ We stopped selling the service at scale only a few people respond to

They have 3 services. All great. But one is a terrible conversation starter.

Cold prospects don’t wake up thinking:
“Wow, I really hope someone offers me a 40-page report today.”

Their prospects literally respond ~2× better to the other 2 services, but outbound wasn’t aligned to that.

So we repositioned around their two strongest conversation starters
They’re simple, clear, and solve urgent problems right now.

2️⃣ We fixed the invisible killer → deliverability

Their audience = mid-market + enterprise.
Enterprise = Microsoft.
Microsoft = “I will evaluate your entire family tree before letting your email through.” 😅

So yep… we’re going to have a different mix of Google + Microsoft inboxes and all these inboxes are purchased by multiple resellers.

3️⃣ We replaced the “quick chat?” CTA with value

Their CTA used to be a meeting request. (in a soft way which is GOOD).

But (especially in the agency space), you’re likely selling something that is “easy” to execute, so the barrier to entry is low.

So we introduced CTAs that give something instead of asking for something:
free strategy session + with campaign ideas

Help with organizing the roundtable + what themes would be the most relevant report on what their prospects are researching

Concrete example, if you’re running an ad agency:

→ “I have analyzed your ads published in the last 90 days. Can I send over a quick audit to decrease the CPL?” 
→ “Would you be open to exploring how we can help you decrease the CPL on your Meta ads?”
GIVE → GIVE → GIVE → before you ASK.

4️⃣ We added intent + timing signals instead of guessing

Before: outbound went out in usual prospecting campaigns
Now: outreach triggers when something meaningful happens.

Signals we added: → new senior hires → hiring for marketing roles → aggressive ad spends → thought leadership indicators → content activity → growth indicators

5️⃣ We refreshed the messaging (just enough)

Not a rewrite — a refresh.
We updated angles based on:

the market’s current priorities
2026 plans
current challenges in their space
This avoids message fatigue

The fun part?
We didn’t change:

❌ the ICP 
❌ the TAM 
❌ the channel 
❌ the core offer 
❌ the sending volume

Takeaway:

When outbound stops performing, people jump to copy first.

But the real leverage is almost always in: → targeting → timing → positioning → offer → infrastructure

Once the system is right, the copy suddenly becomes “amazing.” Even if it’s the same copy you thought was the problem. 😅

Their prospects literally respond ~2× better to the other 2 services, but outbound wasn’t aligned to that.
A tiny repositioning → big impact.

3️⃣ the CTA lacked compelling reasons to meet

In the agency space, you’re likely selling something that is “easy” to execute, so the barrier to entry is low.

What prospects see: “Everyone claims they do outbound, so I assume you’re all the same.”

This is commoditization.
The market is flooded and undifferentiated.

Because of this, you must be SO clear on how you’re different and give them a compelling reason to meet with you.

Concrete example if you’re running an ad agency:

→ “I have analyzed your ads published in the last 90 days. Can I send over a quick audit to decrease the CPL?”

→ “Would you be open to exploring how we can help you decrease the CPL on your Meta ads?”

#1 gives them something valuable for free.

GIVE → GIVE → GIVE → before you ASK.

4️⃣ They weren’t using any intent signals
General prospecting campaigns are good.

But if you’re only doing that, you don’t have any “always-on” campaigns that work 24/7 and indicate a buying window.

So we layered in:
→ new hires
→ accounts scaling ads
→ recent leadership hires
→ thought leaders actively posting/speaking at conferences

You can use Clay Apollo (and many more) to test and capture these windows.

Same TAM.
Same volume.
Same (good) copy.

I’m confident there’ll be a completely different performance.
Because outbound doesn’t always have just a messaging problem.

It usually has a thought process problem.

Lesson I’m taking forward:

If outbound feels slow, don’t rush to rewrite the emails.

Check the infrastructure.
Check the timing.
Check the offer.
Check the CTA.

Check what buyers actually respond to in the first place.

Fix the system → the copy suddenly “works.”
Funny how that happens. 😅

column3: your follow-up structure is as important as building top of funnel.
column11:
your follow-up structure is as important as building top of funnel. 
most teams spend 80% of their energy on new leads. 
and drop everything after touch 1 or 2:

44% of reps send one follow-up and move on. 
80% of deals need 5+ touches to move forward.

here's how we structure follow-up across three account tiers:

Tier 1: high-value accounts 
8–12 touches over 4–6 weeks. 
manual effort. 3+ channels. 
email → LinkedIn → phone (Orum 🥇, Nooks) → voice note (lemlist) → nurture loop. these accounts are worth 5 hours of your time.

Tier 2: good-fit accounts 
4–6 touches over 3–4 weeks. 
semi-automated. email + Linkedin (Instantly.ai, Heyreach.io) 
if no reply by touch 4 — move to long-term nurture, not the bin.

Tier 3: broad or low-fit list 
2–3 touches. email only. fully automated. 
who opened 3 times? who clicked? 
those accounts move up to Tier 2.

a few things that break this:

→ treating every account the same regardless of tier 
→ repeating the same message on every follow-up instead of adding a new angle 
→ dropping Tier 3 accounts entirely instead of handing them to marketing nurture 
→ never upgrading accounts based on engagement signals

Most important to remember: the tier isn't permanent. 
an account that ignores cold outreach can become Tier 1 the moment they attend a webinar, download a report, or engage with your content.

the motion is a loop. Not a one-way funnel → you can’t get a direct response from everybody

get marketing to work on your leads! 
use 1st party data to score them. 
Not everybody is ready to hop on a call with you. Invite those to your webinars, newsletter.

column3: One of your lowest-hanging fruit in outbound?
column11:
One of your lowest-hanging fruit in outbound?

Knowing timing with relevancy beats everything.

Which is exactly why signal-based, always-on outbound is such an easy win. 🏆

Most teams still run prospecting like this:

Build → send → finish → rebuild → repeat.

We’ve all done it.

But that approach makes it almost guaranteed you’ll miss people at the right time.

Because readiness rarely lines up with when you decide to run a campaign.

It usually shows up when something shifts on their side:

• budget changes • new leadership • pressure to hit numbers • new goals • new problems

Here’s what that means in practice 👇

1️⃣ Signals can tell you WHO is ready, not just who “fits the ICP”

Two companies can look identical on paper.

But only one is:

hiring for Demand Gen
posting thought leadership
running new ads
adding new leaders
changing their GTM team
promoting new initiatives

One is active.
The other is static.

Usual prospecting motion treats everyone the same.
Signal-based outbound differentiates who’s ready and who’s not.

2️⃣ You stop “guessing” and start “reacting”

When a new VP joins…
When a Head of Events gets hired…
When a team scales ad spend…
When leadership suddenly becomes very active online…

That’s your window.
Not next quarter.
Not “when we build the next list.”

Right. Then.
Outbound that responds to real changes simply feels more relevant, because it is.

3️⃣ Your messaging becomes naturally relevant

You don’t need hyper-personalization.
You just need context.

Examples we used:

“Saw you’re hiring for Event Marketing — usually means the team is thinking a lot about pipeline. Could I share a few ideas?”

“Congrats on the new senior hire — would a few simple recommendations around X be helpful?”

“Noticed your ad spend is climbing — if mainstream channels aren’t giving you what you need, I can send a quick idea that’s been working well for similar teams.”

When you know who you’re talking to and what they’re dealing with, the message almost writes itself, especially when you offer something tangible.

4️⃣ You stop exhausting the TAM

Usual prospecting motion = you work the static list you already have.
Signal-based outbound = you run always-on campaigns and surface new leaders, new accounts, and new activity as it happens.

It’s easier on the TAM and better for long-term performance.

5️⃣ Conversion rates lift without changing the copy

This is the part people underestimate.
Same message. Same CTA. Same structure.

But when it hits at the right time, the response rate looks completely different.

TAKEAWAY 🤩

Outbound is hard, and not getting easier
…and there are SO many gimmicks and so many tactics

but you cannot disagree that it’s a good idea to reach out to a prospect 
when there’s a real moment to do so ✌️

column3: How to do outreach like the top 1%
column11:
How to do outreach like the top 1%
(After analysing 1,000,000+ sends in Instantly.ai and lemlist)

Here is what the top campaigns had in common:

It was not the copy.
It was not the tool.
It was the order they did things in.

Here is the 4-step system we now run for every campaign:

Step 1: Fix the car’s engine before you drive the car

Before anyone touches copy, we check the foundation.

↳ Is the targeting actually good, or just filtered by persona and company size?
↳ Is the data accurate and up to date? Do we have a system in place to keep it accurate?
↳ Are emails landing in the inbox at all? Do we have a deliverability system in place?

Don’t spend a week on copy when the segmentation strategy was wrong from day one.
It’s like fixing the colour of the car when the engine doesn’t run.

We use Clay for all signals, enrichment, tiering, and scoring, all in one place.
We use EmailBison and EmailGuard to run our automated email infrastructure.

Step 2: Test ONE thing at a time

New ICP. New angle. New tool. Never all three at once.

↳ Change one variable per test → targeting, copy, sequence structure
↳ If two things change at once, you learn nothing
↳ If you slow down to get the right foundation, you get to the desired outcome faster

Step 3: Build feedback loops

Start paying attention to:

↳ Which segments actually replied (vertical, persona, signal)
↳ Where people stopped responding (which step, on what angle, why)
↳ Which objections came up more than once

If you are building outbound from scratch right now, make learning the #1 KPI.
No meetings booked. Learning.

Step 4: Write down and systemize what works

When something starts performing, document it.
Then systemize it.

↳ Segmentation and targeting logic that worked
↳ Deliverability standards that outperform other patterns
↳ Messaging patterns that came from real conversations

Here is what healthy looks like for reference:

Connection acceptance rate: 30–40% = healthy · 50%+ = strong
Cold email reply rate: 3–8% = stable · 10%+ = strong
Positive reply rate: 8–12% = healthy
Bounce rate: under 3% = safe

If you are below these, the problem is usually in Step 1 or Step 3.
Not the copy.

Outbound gets less exciting once it is structured.
(This is how you know it’s working)

No go-to-market channel does not change that much.
The channel only amplifies what is already working underneath it.
(or what is not)

Do you feel you have everything in place to run truly structured experiments?

Every repetitive task must end in one of two ways: A system… or a new owner.

In the early days, I was doing almost everything.

Things like:

client calls
building Clay tables
writing outbound copy
setting up email infrastructure
buying inboxes one by one
configuring SPF, DKIM & DMARC

(That’s just what the early stage looks like.)
But if I kept doing all that, the company would stay small.

My real job was to replace myself.
Otherwise, we could never hit $1M+ ARR in less than 12 months

Every few months, I looked at my week and asked: what can I should never touch again.

Then I did five things:

Hire people who are better than you at specific things
Replace manual work with systems and automation
Move responsibility to the team instead of holding it yourself
Stop doing tasks someone else can do
Shift your focus from doing the work → improving the business

Example:

I do not write outbound copy anymore. Specialists do that now.
I do not run client meetings anymore. The team owns them, start to finish.
I do not build outbound infrastructure anymore. We have documented systems for that.

That shift is the whole point.

Your role moves from working in the business to working on the business.

Only happens if you keep replacing yourself.

What part of your week should end in a system or a new owner next?
